issues.legal_issue: Government allotments of public land to housing societies are arbitrary when the selection criterion is not disclosed to all applicants and is not applied uniformly.
material_facts: The government said allotments would be made on a first-come, first-served basis, but the public notice inviting applications did not disclose that criterion.
Some societies had applied directly to the ministry, while others applied through the registrar; applicants were not told that both routes would be considered.
The first-come, first-served criterion was not applied uniformly, and the government acknowledged that it had not been universally followed.
The challenged allotments were made to a selected group of societies, and the High Court quashed them on arbitrariness grounds.
issues.conclusion: The allotments violated Article 14 and were properly quashed; the claimed compliance of some societies with the criterion did not cure the failure to disclose it to all applicants.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 prohibits arbitrary and discriminatory state action. Where public land is allocated by reference to a selection criterion, applicants must be informed of that criterion and it must be applied consistently; non-disclosure to all applicants is a defect that cannot be cured by showing that some selected applicants complied with it. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.public_land_allotment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning government allotments of public land to housing societies.
predicates.selection_basis_not_disclosed: The government did not inform all applicant societies of the criterion it would use to select recipients.
predicates.selection_basis_not_applied_uniformly: The government did not apply the announced selection criterion uniformly to applicant societies.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns government allotments of public land and the selection basis was neither disclosed to all applicants nor applied uniformly, the allotment order is quashed.

issues.legal_issue: A court cannot compel allotment of public land to particular applicant societies without a comparative assessment of applicants where the government retains the choice to reserve the land for its own needs or allocate it for housing.
material_facts: The land was government-owned nazul land, not land acquired for housing purposes.
The High Court left the government free to decide whether to reserve the land for government needs or allot it to housing societies.
The comparative merits of all applicant societies had not been assessed.
The non-allottee societies sought directions requiring the government to allot land to them.
issues.conclusion: The court declined to direct allotment to the non-allottee societies; the government retained the option to reserve the land or consider allotment after assessing applicants comparatively.
issues.legal_principle: The government may decide whether nazul land is to be retained for its own requirements or allotted for housing. A court cannot direct allotment to particular applicants without evaluation of the comparative merits of all relevant applicants. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.non_allottee_allocation_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal by applicants who were not allotted public land and who seek a direction requiring allotment to them.
predicates.land_not_acquired_for_housing: The land was government-owned land that had not been acquired for housing purposes.
predicates.comparative_merits_not_assessed: The government had not comparatively evaluated the merits of all applicant societies.

issues.definition: When non-allottee applicants seek a directed allotment of government land that was not acquired for housing and the applicants’ comparative merits have not been assessed, no specific allotment direction is made.

issues.legal_issue: The government must compensate societies for the loss of interest on land-price deposits when its arbitrary allotments are cancelled and the societies do not receive the land.
material_facts: The government had received deposits from societies toward the cost of the land.
The allotments were cancelled because the government had acted arbitrarily.
The government had the benefit of the deposited money while the societies suffered loss of interest.
The court made repayment with interest conditional on the government deciding not to allot the land to the societies or allotting it only to societies eligible under the applicable norms.
issues.conclusion: If the government decides not to allot the land to the depositing societies, or excludes some of them while allotting it only to eligible societies, it must refund the affected societies’ deposits with interest from the date of deposit until refund.
issues.legal_principle: A government whose arbitrariness leads to cancellation of allotments must restore the money it received and compensate for the loss of interest where it has had the benefit of the deposits. No statutory provision or earlier case is relied on for this direction.

predicates.appeal_from_cancelled_land_allotment: The proceeding is an appeal arising from cancellation of government land allotments.
predicates.government_received_deposits: The government received deposits from societies toward the cost of the land and retained their benefit.
predicates.government_does_not_allocate_to_all_depo: The government decides not to allot the land to all societies that made deposits, including by allotting only to societies that meet the applicable criteria.

issues.definition: When an appeal follows cancellation of land allotments, the government received and benefited from deposits, and it does not allot land to all depositing societies, the deposits must be refunded with interest.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court does not err by examining government files without giving affected allottees access to them when the files are examined to assess a challenge to the allotments.
material_facts: The High Court examined the original government files concerning the allotments to assess whether the allegations of arbitrariness and discrimination were supported.
The affected allottee societies did not have access to those files or an opportunity to respond to the adverse material in them.
The High Court relied on the files to test the challenge before it, rather than to effect a government cancellation by an indirect method.
issues.conclusion: The High Court committed no error by examining the files without making them accessible to the affected societies.
issues.legal_principle: A court may inspect administrative files to determine whether a challenge to government action is supported by the record; such inspection is not an impermissible indirect cancellation where the court is exercising its reviewing function. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.administrative_allotment_appeal: The proceeding is an appeal concerning government allotments of public land.
predicates.court_inspected_government_files: The reviewing court examined government files relating to the challenged administrative action.
predicates.inspection_tested_the_challenge: The court used the files to assess the allegations raised in the challenge.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns government allotments and the court inspects government files to assess the challenge, the inspection is not an error.
